prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture collapsed to DONE on every episode, with 0.000 on both seeds. The cause looks structural. The target channels are rolled 4 columns, with wrap-around, so the target for column x appears at observed column x+4. The stem uses only 1x1 convolutions and the trunk has two 3x3 convolutions, so it sees just ±2 columns and cannot reach the shifted target. It also cannot follow the wrap. Almost every placement therefore earns a negative reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The first priority is to line up target features with build features without hard-coding the shift. One option stacks every circular x-shift of the target-derived channels before a learned 1x1 stem. This is only slicing and concatenation, and it amounts to a learned circular full-width convolution. Another lets attention learn the offset through a circular relative-position bias. Recipe changes come second; with the default recipe there are only about 32 updates.

### Round 2
The observation shows the target rolled 4 columns, so it doesn't line up with the build. Without a fix the network never learns a useful placement and every episode ends in an immediate DONE (start 0.000; the attention with relative bias also scored 0.000). Giving a learned 1x1 stem every circular x-shift of the target channels fixes this: it scored 0.42 with the default recipe and 0.72 with more, smaller updates (128 envs, 3 epochs, gamma 0.97). Seed spread is large (0.83 vs 0.60, 0.53 vs 0.31), so the recipe gain is likely real but noisy. In r1c2, training success was still rising at the end (0.74 to 0.80), and each trial used about 90 of the 900 seconds allowed. So the limit is samples and updates, not time. Dev IoU is 0.97 with few extra cells, so the misses are small exactness errors. These probably come from landing heights under multi-cell footprints, where max/min/avg pooling throws away which cell holds which value. Next: more updates or samples, and a footprint head that sees each cell.

### Round 3
Aligning the target is what makes the agent work. Every trial that feeds the network circular x-shifts of the target learns to place bricks, and the trial without them (and the attention trial r1c3) collapsed to DONE. Once a seed works it builds well: three seeds reached 0.83–0.84 dev success. The problem is reliability. Under the 128-env recipes, 2 of 6 seeds collapsed to an immediate DONE, and r2c2's smaller batches (more, noisier updates) lost both seeds. The likely cause is timing. Early random placements earn negative reward, so DONE (reward 0) gets reinforced before the network learns which shift is the true one. The best mean, 0.72 for r1c2, is probably partly luck in which seeds survived. Two fixes follow. One is to slow the collapse with a larger entropy bonus. The other is to make the shift easier to find: a small learned layer, shared across channels, that mixes the 8 shifts, so the gradient for the correct shift pools over all target channels. The third candidate combines both.

### Round 4
Every model that learned anything uses some way of undoing the target shift: a stack of shifted copies or a learned shift gate. Without it, the agent quickly learns to choose DONE before placing anything. Seed 0 seems to top out at about 0.84 under any reasonable setup. Seed 1 decides the mean: across trials it scored 0.31, 0.60, 0, 0, 0, 0.23, 0.08 and 0.61. The best result, r3c3 (0.72), is the shared shift gate plus entropy 0.03, the only setup where seed 1 got above 0.6. Its training success was still rising at the end. Things that hurt stability: 64 envs (both seeds collapsed) and 2 PPO epochs (one seed collapsed). With 128 envs both seeds survived. The useful moves are those that make seed 1 align faster or collapse later. All three candidates keep r3c3 and change one thing: a stronger entropy bonus, more parallel worlds per update at the same number of updates, or more gate mixtures.

## Trial it ended with
name: shift gate + entropy 0.05
hypothesis: Same as r3c3, but the entropy coefficient rises from 0.03 to the maximum, 0.05. Raising it from 0.01 to 0.03 lifted the weak seed from collapse to 0.23 (full stack) and to 0.61 (gate). More entropy should delay the early collapse onto DONE further, so the weak seed reaches seed 0's level of about 0.84. Refuted if the 2-seed mean is not above 0.72, or if seed 0 falls clearly below 0.8.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 states the rule directly: "The target channels are rolled 4 columns, with wrap-around, so the target for column x appears at observed column x+4." That covers what changes (the target channels), how much (4 columns), which way (toward higher x) and the wrap-around. Round 2 says it again: "The observation shows the target rolled 4 columns."
